newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Poll gives Bulgaria opposition UDF 53.3 pct support.
newsitem.headline: Poll gives Bulgaria opposition UDF 53.3 pct support.

text.p: Bulgaria's opposition coalition, hoping to translate mass protests into victory in April elections, would win two thirds of parliamentary seats if polls were held now, a survey published on Monday showed.

The opinion poll by the NOEMA agency, published by the Standart daily, confirmed predictions by other polling agencies over the weekend showing a sharp rise in support for the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), while the outgoing Socialist majority was widely blamed for the country's severe economic crisis.
The poll gave the Socialists 14.2 percent, and the UDF 53.3 percent, plus 11.3 percent for its coalition allies, giving a total of 64.6 percent.

The Socialists won parliamentary elections in December 1994 but lost support as the economy worsened. After Prime Minister Zhan Videnov resigned in December they insisted on forming a new cabinet but were eventually persuaded to agree to elections after 30 consecutive days of mass nationwide protests.

The NOEMA poll also showed President Petar Stoyanov, who brokered the agreement on early elections, was Bulgaria's most popular politician, followed by Sofia's UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski, whom Stoyanov is expected to name as interim prime minister this week.
The poll put support for the UDF's main allies, the People's Union and the ethnic Turkish Movement for Rights and Freedoms, at 6.4 percent and 4.9 percent respectively.
Twenty-one percent of the electorate said they would not vote at all.

Polling agency MBMD said at the weekend defections from the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) to a new Euro-Left movement could split the Socialist vote to eight percent for the BSP and seven percent for the Euro-Left.
The caretaker cabinet will govern until a new government is formed after elections due by April 20.
Parliament is to meet on Wednesday to debate changes in the electoral law.

The Socialists boycotted parliament on Thursday and Friday but say they will return for this session, which will also discuss amendments to the income tax law and a bill giving the caretaker government a mandate to borrow funds for grain imports and to negotiate with the International Monetary Fund.
Socialist party leader Georgi Parvanov said on Saturday the Socialists opposed widening the powers of the caretaker cabinet, which strictly is mandated only to organise the elections.
